touches.text: CODEMOTHER DEVICE (cairn/devices/codemother/)
tester

WHY: Law 8: nothing enters proven-space without a proof a hollow build couldn't pass, and the verdict must come from a hand the builder did not guide. A green cannot be self-granted. A machine under CodeMother, not a device: CodeMother does not build, so the tester inside her puts no builder between a build and its verdict, and nothing here needs its own process in the rack, since each proof run is its own process already.
Runs a proof as its own process and writes a validation record (claim, caller, date, method, verdict, evidence, falsifier, horizon).
Hollow runs: proves a proof goes red when the build is removed.
Seals: one current validation per proof, beside the proof. A seal holds while the code it measured is unchanged.

A seal is host independent: one record per proof, whichever box asks. Seals are made by one sealing machine in the cairn device, and there is only ever one cairn (until a laptop dies and a backup takes over), so there is one sealer. A box that is not cairn's home asks the sealer instead of writing its own seal. Akien 2026-11-13, answering Q#90 (a Windows reseal of a mixed proof overwrote the Linux seal, measured 2026-11-12): "then we have to invent a way for seals to be host independent. one way would be to create a sealing machine in cairn. there's only ever one cairn until we have a laptop die and have to fail over to a backup".

Commit: the proofs of the component the ticket changed, since RULE 1 bounds a change to its component. Passing them puts the component in service, yellow: proven where it changed, not yet measured against what depends on it. Akien: "being put in service only requires that it's the best we can do now. only requires 80% trust."

There is no central supervisor. Each part starts what it needs by trying to use it: sending a message starts the bus if it is down, a message arriving wakes its shim, the shim wakes its device. Many very small supervisors, each one detect-and-start. WHY: a supervisor is one more thing to keep up, and the system must come up from any part that is touched.
The detect-and-start lives in one tool, the waker, and it sits inside connect: every client's connect is a wake attempt, so no caller can forget one. A probe watches and reports; the waker acts.
launcher (machine)
INTENTION:
INTENTION:
Messages sit in a SMALL buffer in memory. WHY: in memory is faster.

A shim waking its device never takes more than 60 s. A sync caller waits at most 60 s for the wake, then gets "not now" back; a wake that misses 60 s is a trouble. 600 s is the limit for an inference call to come back, not for a wake.
The shim always starts its device. Nothing else does.
It wakes the device when it's not running and is needed.
If the device won't come up, the shim retries; after many retries it files a trouble ticket for Akien and CC. This holds for every wake: a request, a pulse, the sleep token.

Scratch bus: a proof needs a bus it controls (a real store, stub devices, nobody live listening), so the cairn device publishes scratch_bus, the way db_domain's client carries scratch(). Akien 2026-11-12, answering Q#86 (8 proof imports of the bus machine in tester, codemother and librarian, measured 2026-11-11): "works for me". 2.3.8Every device has the panes the base shim defines (17.1.3.5.2), drawn by the web server (15):
scratch: a proof's throwaway temp dirs and worktrees, cleaned up by the door. WHY: a run must leave nothing behind (4.3.1.7). USERS: the tester.
